lead: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE, also deanol, DMEA) is an ingredient in some skin-care gels and creams sold for firming and smoothing aging skin. People use it topically in the hope of tighter-looking skin, softer fine lines on the forehead and around the eyes, and a fuller lip shape.[3] It is also sold as the bitartrate salt in oral nootropic supplements.[1][2]

DMAE is an analog of choline and a precursor of acetylcholine. A 2005 review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology proposed that acetylcholine acts as a cytokine-like signal in skin that regulates cell proliferation, differentiation and secretion, which could underlie DMAE's cutaneous activity.[3] The review summarised a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of a 3% DMAE facial gel applied daily for 16 weeks, which reported improvements in forehead lines and fine periorbital wrinkles and in lip shape and fullness.[3]

Outside cosmetics, DMAE is mainly an industrial chemical used as a curing agent for polyurethanes and epoxy resins and as an intermediate for other compounds.[1][2] In the mid-20th century and 1970s it was also studied as a drug, including in tardive dyskinesia trials.[4][16][17]

angle.text: DMAE gels and creams are applied to the face and neck by people wanting a firmer, smoother look. In the main published trial, a 3% gel used daily for 16 weeks was associated with improved forehead lines, fine lines around the eyes, lip fullness and overall appearance.

infobox: Bitartrate salt (about 37% DMAE) in supplements; topical cosmetic ingredient[2]

paras: DMAE is a bifunctional molecule carrying a tertiary amine and a primary alcohol. It is prepared industrially by ethoxylation of dimethylamine, or by reaction of dimethylamine with ethylene oxide, and is a flammable, corrosive liquid with a fishy odour that mixes readily with water.[2][1] Wikipedia lists a boiling point of about 134 degrees Celsius and a flash point of about 39 degrees.[2] Reported oral LD50 in rats is around 1 to 2 g per kg depending on the source.[1][2]

The bitartrate salt used in supplements supplies about 37 percent DMAE by weight.[2] DMAE is also a precursor to 2-dimethylaminoethyl chloride and its acrylate ester is used as a flocculating agent.[2] Researchers studying cell membranes have used dimethylethanolamine as a substrate in phospholipid methylation experiments, as an intermediate between phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine.[21]

The 2005 review describes DMAE as a choline analog and precursor of acetylcholine. It notes growing evidence that acetylcholine acts as a ubiquitous cytokine-like molecule regulating proliferation, differentiation, movement and secretion of cells in a paracrine and autocrine way, and suggests this modulatory role may contribute to DMAE's skin activity.[3]

Product marketing often describes DMAE as acting on muscle tone beneath the skin to produce a lifting effect; the published review frames the activity in terms of cell-signalling rather than muscle contraction.[3]

Animal research has examined how deanol is metabolised in rat brain and whether it affects acetylcholine synthesis, a topic cited in T Nation's supplement references.[11] Wikipedia notes animal studies suggesting possible benefit for spatial and working memory and reports no human trial results for the nootropic use.[2]

Cosmetic products use DMAE, often as the bitartrate salt at low percentage concentrations, as a skin-firming ingredient; Grokipedia describes concentrations up to about 3 percent.[1] Manufacturers and proponents describe it as tightening sagging skin and improving tone.[2] The studied form was a 3% facial gel applied daily.[3]

In the trial, the areas assessed included forehead lines, periorbital wrinkles, lip shape and fullness, under-eye dark circles, nasolabial folds, neck sagging and neck firmness, so users interested in lower-face and neck contour were among the intended audience.[3]

DMAE bitartrate is sold as an oral nootropic. Animal studies cited by Wikipedia suggest possible benefit for spatial and working memory, and a pyroglutamate form has been studied against scopolamine-induced memory deficits.[2] Deanol bitartrate also appears in stimulant-style supplement blends, such as one T Nation forum thread that lists 17 mg per serving alongside caffeine and yohimbe extract.[10]

Deanol appears in the medical literature from at least 1959 as a drug.[9] In the 1970s it was tested in tardive dyskinesia, Huntington's chorea, L-dopa-induced dyskinesia and senile dementia, with randomized trials published from 1977 to 1981.[16][17][19][15][18][20] A 1999 meta-analysis found that deanol was no more effective than placebo for tardive dyskinesia, and Cochrane reviews of cholinergic drugs for the condition covered deanol among others.[13][4][12][14]
Its cosmetic profile rose after the 2005 dermatology review that summarised the 16-week gel trial.[3]

Concentrated DMAE is classified under GHS as corrosive and acutely toxic by several routes, with hazard statements for skin burns and eye damage. This is an industrial-handling classification and does not directly describe finished cosmetic products.[2][1] Wikipedia cites a 2002 US National Toxicology Program review of its toxicological literature without summarising the findings.[2]

In the cosmetic trial, application of the 3% gel was reported as well tolerated.[3] A 1979 report on high oral doses described mood changes in 8 of 38 patients (five depressed, three hypomanic), seven of whom had histories of affective symptoms.[8]
DMAE is rarely discussed as a standalone item on appearance forums. On T Nation it appears mainly as an ingredient (deanol bitartrate) in stimulant-style and mood supplements.[10][11]

A randomized, placebo-controlled study reviewed in 2005 tested a 3% DMAE facial gel applied daily for 16 weeks. It was reported as safe and efficacious (p < 0.05) for forehead lines and periorbital fine wrinkles and for lip shape, fullness and the overall appearance of aging skin. Effects did not regress during a 2-week stop. Trends (p between 0.05 and 0.1) were seen for coarse wrinkles, under-eye dark circles, nasolabial folds, sagging neck skin and neck firmness, and application was well tolerated.[3]

A registered phase 2 study (44 participants, completed 2025) tested a serum and cream combining GABA, DMAE, cysteamine and bakuchiol for skin whitening and anti-aging; because several ingredients were combined, it does not isolate DMAE's effect.[7]

Oral deanol was studied in the 1970s and 1980s in tardive dyskinesia, with randomized trials and Cochrane reviews of cholinergic drugs covering it; a double-blind crossover trial in nine patients with Huntington's chorea reported no change in hyperkinesia. These concern movement disorders, not skin.[4][16][17][19][15] One report described mood changes in 8 of 38 patients at high oral doses.[8]

name: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE)

card.summary: Industrial amino alcohol used in skin-firming creams and sold as a nootropic; no human trial isolates its skin effect.
card.note: Concentrated DMAE is a corrosive industrial chemical; cosmetic claims lack published human trials.

quick.overview:
DMAE is mostly an industrial chemical used in plastics and resins. It also appears in some firming skin-care products and in oral nootropic supplements.
No human trial results have been reported for either use, so claims about skin tightening rest on marketing.
quick.mechanism: The way DMAE might affect skin or the brain is not established. Animal studies point to possible memory effects, while no mechanism for skin firming is documented.
quick.risks: The pure liquid is flammable and corrosive and carries hazard warnings. Safety data for cosmetic or supplement use in people are lacking.
